title: How Does a 200,000-Ton Steel Ship Float?

research.summary: Archimedes' principle: a body in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. A ship sinks into the water until the weight of the displaced water equals the ship's total weight; then it floats. A solid steel block (density ~7,850 kg/m3) is far denser than seawater (~1,025 kg/m3) and sinks, but the same steel shaped into a hollow hull encloses a large volume of air, so the hull's average density is below that of water and it can displace its own weight before submerging. Large container ships exceed 200,000 tonnes deadweight; aircraft carriers (~100,000 t) float by the same principle.
facts_checked: Buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid (Archimedes' principle).
A floating ship displaces a mass of water equal to its own mass.
Steel density ~7,850 kg/m3 vs seawater ~1,025 kg/m3: a solid block sinks; a hollow hull with average density below water floats.
Largest container ships exceed 200,000 t deadweight; a modern supercarrier displaces roughly 100,000 t.

scenes.narration: A massive cargo ship can weigh over 200,000 tons,
scenes.storyboard: HOOK. Dramatic aerial shot of an enormous container ship stacked with colorful containers, cutting through the ocean with a white wake.

scenes.narration: so how does something made mostly of steel float instead of sinking?
scenes.storyboard: The camera glides down to the waterline along the giant steel hull, then dips below the surface to reveal the red underwater hull.
scenes.camera: descend to the waterline and dip under

scenes.narration: The secret is displacement. When a ship enters the water, its enormous hull pushes water out of the way.
scenes.storyboard: Classic Archimedes demo: Nova lowers a steel model ship into a full glass tank; the water level rises and spills into a beaker on a scale - the displaced water.
scenes.camera: side view of the tank, push toward the overflow

scenes.narration: That displaced water creates an upward force called buoyancy. As long as this upward force balances the ship's weight, it floats.
scenes.storyboard: Back to the real ship, sea made see-through: water pressure arrows push on the submerged hull; a big BUOYANCY arrow grows until it equals the WEIGHT arrow; the ship settles and floats.

scenes.narration: But here's the interesting part. Ships aren't solid blocks of steel.
scenes.storyboard: Two glass tanks: a solid steel block plunges to the bottom; the same amount of steel shaped as a hollow hull floats.

scenes.narration: Their hollow hulls contain enormous amounts of air, making their overall density much lower than solid steel.
scenes.storyboard: Cutaway of the container ship: double bottom, bulkheads, cargo holds with containers, engine room - and the large air-filled spaces glowing light blue. Label: average density lower than water.

scenes.narration: That's why even the biggest ships can float across the ocean.
scenes.storyboard: Underwater view: the huge red hull and propeller pass overhead in deep blue water with bubbles.

scenes.narration: And the same principle allows tiny objects and enormous aircraft carriers to stay afloat.
scenes.storyboard: A gigantic aircraft carrier floats on the ocean; aerial cinematic orbit over the flight deck.
Wide shot of the cargo ship sailing into a golden sunset. Final title PHYSICS IS INCREDIBLE. with small HOWSTUFF branding.
